newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Shell R'dam unit to make less fuel oil, more gas oil.
newsitem.headline: Shell R'dam unit to make less fuel oil, more gas oil.

text.p: Shell's new 3.3 billion guilder ($1.7 billion) complex at Pernis in Rotterdam will lead to a 1.4 million tonne fall in the annual output of fuel oil, Shell told a news conference on Wednesday.

The "Per+" complex, expected to be fully operational by early autumn, is designed to process more high sulphur crude oil and produce a larger proportion of low sulphur products, principally middle distillates, the company said.
The refinery as a whole will continue to process around 17.9 million tonnes of crude oil per year, but the proportion of high sulphur crude input will rise by over 30 percent to 15.0 million tonnes.
The proportion of low sulphur crude will fall by almost 40 percent to 2.8 million tonnes.
But sulphur content in all products will fall from 150,000 tonnes to 100,000 tonnes per year, Shell said.
White product output (gasoline, naphtha and middle distillate) will rise on average nine percent to 14.0 million tonnes and fuel oil output will fall by 40 percent to 2.1 million tonnes per year.
The new complex involves three principle additions to the Pernis refinery -- a hydrocracking unit, a gasification unit producing hydrogen and a 115 megawatt power generating plant.
Shell also plans to close one of its two catalytic crackers, most likely in autumn.
Shell says the Per+ complex puts it a step ahead of its rivals by introducing a gasification unit which will break down heavy residues in the production of hydrogen to feed its hydrocracker.
"The process involves effectively pulling apart the residue," said Shell technology manager Krijn de Jong.
The hydrocracker, with a throughput of 8,000 tonnes per stream day, is the largest of its kind in the world.It came onstream last week.
It's role is to increase the flexibility of Shell's production and allow it to produce more middle distillate and less gasoline to suit the European oil product markets.
Shell predicts that by the year 2005, diesel demand in Europe, at about 125 million tonnes, will outstrip that for gasoline.
